_about.purpose: Golden multilingual dataset for books/manifesto classification.
_about.principle: The distinction is FUNCTIONAL, not topical. A political novel is books. A history of a revolution is books. A text calling for that revolution is manifesto. 'Mentions politics' contributes nothing; 'demands something' does.
_about.note: Each case carries the destination it must receive and why. Cases marked ambiguous=true are genuinely hard and are asserted only for low confidence, not for a particular answer -- pretending they have an obvious answer would make the suite lie about how good the classifier is.

cases.title: The House on the Marsh
cases.rationale: Narrative prose with dialogue and chapter structure. The dominant act is to tell a story.
cases.text:
CHAPTER I

In the year 1849 my father took the house on the marsh, and it is of that winter, and of what befell us there, that I mean to give an account.

He said, when we first came in sight of it, that no man had lived there in twenty years. My sister replied that she could well believe it. The wind came off the water and the shutters answered it all night.

CHAPTER II

Once upon a time, my grandmother used to say, the marsh had been good land. She said it in the way people say things they do not expect to be believed.

In the first place the roof leaked; in the second, the well had gone brackish. My father wrote to the agent and received no reply. He whispered to my mother that we should not stay past spring, and she answered that we had nowhere else to go.

CHAPTER III

It was in February that I first saw the light across the water. I told no one. For example, I did not tell my sister, who would have laughed, nor my mother, who would have wept.

The narrator of this account is now an old man, and he sets it down as he remembers it, which is not necessarily as it was.

cases.title: The Agitator: A Novel of the Strike
cases.rationale: A NOVEL about politics. Its subject is political, its function is narrative. This is the single most important negative case in the set: topic must not decide destination.
cases.text:
CHAPTER I

When Ellen came down to the gate that morning the men were already standing in the road, and she knew from the way they stood that the strike had begun.

He said, "They will not open the sheds today." She replied that she had heard as much from her brother, who had it from the foreman.

CHAPTER II

In the year 1889 the mills at Renforth employed four hundred men. It has often been argued that the strike of that autumn was inevitable; the evidence suggests that it was very nearly averted.

Ellen watched her father cross the yard. He whispered something to the older Hanlon, who laughed without pleasure. According to the newspapers, the owners had offered a farthing; according to the men, they had offered nothing at all.

CHAPTER III

The narrator has tried to set down what happened at Renforth without deciding who was right. For example, the burning of the gatehouse has been described as an accident and as arson, and he does not know which it was.

In the first place the winter came early that year. In the second, the fund was exhausted by December. What followed, he describes as he saw it.

cases.title: A History of the Revolution of 1848
cases.rationale: A history OF a revolution. Explains and narrates; does not call for anything.
cases.text:
CHAPTER I

In the year 1848 the governments of Europe were confronted, within a period of four months, with insurrections in Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Milan, and Budapest. It has often been argued that these were a single movement; the evidence suggests otherwise.

According to Tocqueville, who was present, the Parisian rising of February took the ministry entirely by surprise. This chapter examines that claim.

CHAPTER II

In the first place, the economic distress of 1846 and 1847 must be considered. For example, the price of bread in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine rose by more than half between the harvests.

The evidence shows that the provisional government was assembled within thirty hours. This book aims to explain how that was possible, and to leave to others the question whether it was wise.

CHAPTER III

We shall see in a later chapter that the June days destroyed what February had made. Ibid., p. 212. The historian describes these events with the advantage of knowing how they ended, which the participants did not.

cases.title: Manifesto of the Communist Party
cases.rationale: Declares a doctrine, names an adversary, demands specific changes, and calls explicitly for action.
cases.text:
MANIFESTO OF THE COMMUNIST PARTY

A spectre is haunting Europe. All the Powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise it.

It is high time that Communists should openly, in the face of the whole world, publish their views, their aims, and their tendencies.

We declare openly that our ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. We demand the abolition of property in land and the application of all rents of land to public purposes.

Our enemies are the bourgeoisie, and we name them. We must destroy the conditions that produced them. Every member of the association shall contribute according to their ability.

Down with the rule of capital. We proclaim a new era. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.

Workers of the world, unite!

cases.title: Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen
cases.rationale: A founding declaration: numbered articles, prescriptive, establishes duties and rights.
cases.text:
DÉCLARATION DES DROITS DE L'HOMME ET DU CITOYEN

Nous déclarons que l'ignorance, l'oubli ou le mépris des droits de l'homme sont les seules causes des malheurs publics.

Article premier. — Les hommes naissent et demeurent libres et égaux en droits. Les distinctions sociales ne peuvent être fondées que sur l'utilité commune.

Article II. — Le but de toute association politique est la conservation des droits naturels et imprescriptibles de l'homme.

Article III. — Le principe de toute souveraineté réside essentiellement dans la Nation. Nul corps, nul individu ne peut exercer d'autorité qui n'en émane expressément.

Article IV. — Tout citoyen doit obéissance à la loi. Nul ne peut être inquiété pour ses opinions.

Nous proclamons ces principes en présence et sous les auspices de l'Être suprême. Nous exigeons qu'ils soient respectés par tous les pouvoirs constitués.

cases.title: Traité de la connaissance des passions
cases.rationale: Analytical philosophy: argues and explains rather than mobilizes. Philosophy without a collective programme is books.
cases.text:
CHAPITRE PREMIER

Les passions, considérées en elles-mêmes, ne sont ni bonnes ni mauvaises. C'est dans leur ordonnance que consiste la vertu, et les philosophes des écoles anciennes s'accordaient sur ce point, quelque divisés qu'ils fussent ensuite.

On a souvent soutenu que les stoïciens tenaient les passions pour des erreurs de jugement. Par exemple, Sénèque le dit en plusieurs endroits, et se contredit ailleurs.

CHAPITRE II

Nous examinerons d'abord la nature de l'appétit, puis celle de la crainte. Selon Aristote, nous devenons justes en faisant des actions justes, et non par le raisonnement seul.

Ce livre vise à expliquer plutôt qu'à prescrire. Il était une fois d'usage de traiter ces matières par des maximes; nous préférons l'analyse.

CHAPITRE III

Il faut distinguer ici deux sens du mot. On a remarqué que le même auteur décrit les passions comme des maladies dans un endroit et comme des mouvements de l'âme dans un autre.

cases.title: Manifeste du surréalisme
cases.rationale: An artistic manifesto: proclaims a movement, prescribes rules for its members, names adversaries, calls for action.
cases.text:
MANIFESTE DU SURRÉALISME

Nous déclarons que l'imagination seule rend compte de ce qui peut être. Le surréalisme repose sur la croyance à la réalité supérieure de certaines formes d'associations négligées jusqu'à lui.

Nous exigeons la fin du règne de la logique. Il faut détruire les habitudes de l'esprit qui nous enchaînent.

Article premier. — La production surréaliste est automatique.
Article II. — Nul ne peut se réclamer du mouvement sans y adhérer pleinement.
Article III. — Le rêve prime sur l'observation.

Nous proclamons une ère nouvelle. Tout membre de l'association doit se garder de la littérature de circonstance. Nos ennemis sont ceux qui font profession de bon sens.

À bas les académies. Debout, les esprits libres ! Nous appelons chacun à l'action immédiate et à la transformation de la vie. Vive le surréalisme !

cases.title: Recueil de sonnets
cases.rationale: Poetry: short and non-narrative, which is exactly the shape a length-based or lexical heuristic mistakes for a manifesto. Catalogue form must carry it.
cases.text:
SONNETS

I

Quand vous serez bien vieille, au soir, à la chandelle,
Assise auprès du feu, dévidant et filant,
Direz, chantant mes vers, en vous émerveillant :
Ronsard me célébrait du temps que j'étais belle.

II

Le temps s'en va, le temps s'en va, ma dame ;
Las ! le temps non, mais nous nous en allons,
Et tôt serons étendus sous la lame.

III

Je n'ai plus que les os, un squelette je semble,
Décharné, dénervé, démusclé, dépoulpé,
Que le trait de la mort sans pardon a frappé.

IV

Comme on voit sur la branche au mois de mai la rose,
En sa belle jeunesse, en sa première fleur,
Rendre le ciel jaloux de sa vive couleur.

cases.title: Fünfundneunzig Thesen
cases.rationale: Numbered theses that prescribe doctrine and name what must change. Doctrinal and programmatic, not expository.
cases.text:
DISPUTATION ZUR ERLÄUTERUNG DER KRAFT DER ABLÄSSE

Wir erklären, dass die folgenden Sätze zur Erörterung gestellt werden.

1. Da unser Herr und Meister Jesus Christus spricht "Tut Buße", hat er gewollt, dass das ganze Leben der Gläubigen Buße sein soll.

2. Dieses Wort kann nicht von der sakramentalen Buße verstanden werden.

3. Wir fordern, dass die innere Buße nichts ist, wenn sie nicht äußerlich mancherlei Abtötung des Fleisches wirkt.

4. Jeder Christ soll wissen, dass ihm Vergebung ohne Ablassbriefe zuteil wird.

5. Nieder mit dem Handel, der die Gnade zur Ware macht. Unsere Feinde sind jene, die aus der Furcht der Gläubigen Gewinn ziehen.

Es lebe die Wahrheit des Evangeliums. Wir rufen jeden Christenmenschen auf, diese Sätze zu prüfen und danach zu handeln.

cases.title: Abhandlung über die Bewegung der Himmelskörper
cases.rationale: A scientific treatise: demonstrative and explanatory throughout.
cases.text:
KAPITEL I

Im Jahre 1609 wurde die erste Beobachtung angestellt, von der in dieser Abhandlung die Rede sein wird. Es ist oft behauptet worden, dass die Bahnen der Planeten Kreise seien; die Beobachtungen zeigen etwas anderes.

Nach Kepler verhalten sich die Quadrate der Umlaufzeiten wie die Kuben der mittleren Entfernungen. Zum Beispiel ergibt die Rechnung für den Mars eine Abweichung von acht Bogenminuten.

KAPITEL II

Wir werden zunächst die Beobachtungen darstellen und sodann die Folgerungen prüfen. Dieses Buch will erklären, nicht vorschreiben.

Der Verfasser beschreibt hier, was er gemessen hat, und überlässt die Deutung anderen. Ebenda, S. 44.

KAPITEL III

Es hat sich gezeigt, dass die Abweichung nicht aus Beobachtungsfehlern erklärt werden kann. Wir werden sehen, dass daraus eine neue Gestalt der Bahn folgt.

cases.title: Constitución de la República
cases.rationale: A founding constitutional text: numbered articles establishing an order and duties.
cases.text:
CONSTITUCIÓN DE LA REPÚBLICA

Nosotros, los representantes del pueblo, declaramos y establecemos la presente Constitución.

Artículo 1. — La soberanía reside en el pueblo, del cual emanan todos los poderes del Estado.

Artículo 2. — Todos los ciudadanos son iguales ante la ley. No se reconocen fueros ni privilegios de nacimiento.

Artículo 3. — Exigimos que ninguna autoridad exceda las facultades que esta Constitución le confiere.

Artículo 4. — Es deber de todo ciudadano defender el orden aquí establecido.

Proclamamos estos principios y llamamos a todos los ciudadanos a sostenerlos. Nuestros enemigos son quienes pretendan restaurar los privilegios abolidos. ¡Viva la República!

cases.title: Viaje a las regiones equinocciales
cases.rationale: Travel narrative: descriptive and observational.
cases.text:
CAPÍTULO I

En el año 1799 emprendimos el viaje del que se da cuenta en este volumen. El lector no encontrará aquí ni programa ni argumento, sino solamente las observaciones que un ojo paciente pudo recoger.

Dijo el piloto que no había visto jamás una costa semejante, y yo le respondí que tampoco yo. Según Bouguer, la misma observación se había hecho un siglo antes.

CAPÍTULO II

En primer lugar, la vegetación cambia con la altura de un modo que merece descripción detallada. Por ejemplo, a los mil quinientos metros desaparecen las palmas.

Este libro pretende consignar lo observado y dejar a otros el trabajo de la explicación. Veremos en un capítulo posterior que este patrón se repite.

CAPÍTULO III

Del interior puedo decir menos. El narrador de una relación anterior describe un lago de gran profundidad, y yo no lo hallé.

cases.title: Manifesto del Futurismo
cases.rationale: An aesthetic manifesto: proclaims a movement, enumerates programmatic points, names enemies, calls for destruction and renewal.
cases.text:
MANIFESTO DEL FUTURISMO

Dichiariamo di voler cantare l'amor del pericolo, l'abitudine all'energia e alla temerità.

1. Noi vogliamo cantare l'amor del pericolo, l'abitudine all'energia e alla temerità.
2. Il coraggio, l'audacia, la ribellione saranno elementi essenziali della nostra poesia.
3. Chiediamo che si distrugga il culto del passato.
4. Ogni membro del movimento deve rifiutare il compromesso con il gusto stabilito.

I nostri nemici sono i professori, gli archeologi, i ciceroni e gli antiquari. Proclamiamo un'era nuova.

Abbasso i musei e le biblioteche. In piedi, spiriti liberi! Chiamiamo ciascuno all'azione immediata e alla trasformazione della vita. Viva il Futurismo!

cases.title: La commedia degli inganni
cases.rationale: Drama: dialogue and stage directions. Another short, non-narrative form a naive heuristic could mistake for a manifesto.
cases.text:
PERSONAGGI

ORAZIO, mercante
BEATRICE, sua figlia
TRUFFALDINO, servitore

ATTO I

SCENA I

Una sala in casa di Orazio.

ORAZIO. Dove sei stato tutta la mattina?
TRUFFALDINO. Dal notaio, padrone, come mi avete ordinato.
ORAZIO. E che disse?
TRUFFALDINO. Disse che l'atto non si può fare senza la firma della signora.

SCENA II

BEATRICE. Ho udito ogni cosa dalla stanza vicina.
ORAZIO. Non era per te.
BEATRICE. Rispose il notaio che senza di me nulla si conclude, e in questo almeno ha ragione.

ATTO II

SCENA I

Una strada. Entra Truffaldino.

TRUFFALDINO. Due padroni, due salari, e un solo stomaco. Chi mi biasima non ha mai avuto fame.

cases.title: Bulla de disciplina ecclesiastica
cases.rationale: A promulgating decree: establishes obligations and prescribes an order. Short by nature, which is exactly why length must not decide.
cases.text:
BULLA DE DISCIPLINA ECCLESIASTICA

Declaramus atque statuimus quae sequuntur, ad perpetuam rei memoriam.

Articulus I. — Omnes clerici ad hanc disciplinam teneantur, nec ulla consuetudine se excusare possint.

Articulus II. — Quod si quis contra haec fecerit, sciat se poenam incursurum esse.

Articulus III. — Omnia quae huic constitutioni adversantur, abolita esse decernimus.

Hostes nostri sunt qui hanc disciplinam contemnunt. Novam aetatem proclamamus. Vocamus omnes fideles ut haec statuta servent atque defendant.

cases.title: Commentarius in libros naturales
cases.rationale: A scholastic commentary: expository and analytical.
cases.text:
CAPUT PRIMUM

In hoc libro tractatur de natura rerum, et quo modo per causas cognoscantur. Saepe dictum est philosophos in hac re dissentire; nos utramque sententiam exponemus.

Secundum Aristotelem, natura est principium motus et quietis. Hoc autem non ita intelligendum est ut quidam interpretati sunt.

CAPUT SECUNDUM

Primo videndum est quid sit materia; deinde quid forma. Exempli gratia, in statua aes est materia, figura vero forma.

Hic liber explicare vult, non praecipere. Auctor ea describit quae observata sunt, et interpretationem aliis relinquit. Ibidem, p. 44.

CAPUT TERTIUM

Videbimus in capite sequenti quomodo haec omnia inter se cohaereant.

cases.title: A Sermon Preached Before the Assembly
cases.rationale: A programmatic sermon: not exposition of scripture but a call to collective action and a naming of adversaries.
cases.text:
A SERMON PREACHED BEFORE THE ASSEMBLY

We declare this day that the covenant has been broken, and that it must be renewed by our own act.

It is the duty of every member of this congregation to put away the works of the oppressor. We demand the release of those imprisoned for conscience.

Our enemies are not flesh and blood only; they are the powers that keep the poor in hunger and call it order. We reject the counsel of patience that has been offered to us.

We must sweep away what has been built upon injustice. A new era begins when this people rises. Every citizen shall be accounted a keeper of his brother.

Arise, and let the assembly be of one mind. We call upon each of you to act, and to act now. Down with the yoke. Long live the covenant.

cases.title: The Life of a Reformer
cases.rationale: A biography OF a political agitator. The subject demands things; the book describes him demanding them.
cases.text:
CHAPTER I

He was born in 1802, in a town whose name he later refused to give. This book aims to describe his life, and not to settle the quarrels that surrounded it.

According to his sister, he learned to read late and then read constantly. It has often been argued that his politics were formed at the mill; the evidence suggests they were formed considerably earlier.

CHAPTER II

In the first place he was not, as his opponents claimed, an uneducated man. For example, his notebooks of 1831 contain long extracts from Bentham.

He said, in a speech his biographer has been unable to verify, that he would rather be hanged than petition again. The historian describes this as characteristic; the evidence shows he petitioned twice more.

CHAPTER III

We shall see in a later chapter how the movement he founded outlived him. Ibid., p. 88. He died in 1867, and the account of his last years rests chiefly on his daughter's diary.

cases.title: A Dictionary of the Sciences
cases.rationale: Reference work: purely expository.
cases.text:
ABERRATION. In optics, the failure of rays to converge at a single focus. It has often been observed that the effect is more marked at the edge of a lens. For example, the achromatic doublet was devised to correct it.

BAROMETER. An instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure. According to Torricelli, who first constructed one, the height of the column varies with the weather.

CALORIC. A supposed substance formerly held to constitute heat. The evidence suggests that this hypothesis is no longer tenable, though it is retained here for the reader's information.

DECLINATION. The angle between magnetic and true north. This work aims to record the accepted definitions and to indicate where authorities differ.

ECLIPSE. The obscuration of one body by another. We shall see under OCCULTATION that the terms are not synonymous.

cases.title: On the Grounds of Political Obligation
cases.rationale: Normative political philosophy that argues for conclusions about what states ought to do without mobilizing anyone. Analytical throughout -- 'This book aims to assess these arguments' -- so it is books, and the classifier is right to be confident.
cases.text:
CHAPTER I

The question of political obligation is the question why anyone should obey. It has often been argued that consent supplies the answer; the difficulty is that almost nobody has consented to anything.

We shall examine three accounts in turn. According to the first, obligation rests on benefit received. This book aims to assess these arguments rather than to adjudicate between the parties who invoke them.

CHAPTER II

It is the duty of the citizen, on the second account, to support institutions that are tolerably just. But it must be shown what tolerably just means, and this has rarely been attempted with any rigour.

We must reject, I think, the view that mere residence constitutes consent. For example, a man born in a state he cannot leave has consented to nothing.

CHAPTER III

The evidence suggests that no single account will serve. We shall see that a plural account, though less tidy, fits the cases better.

cases.title: The Condition of the Universities and What Must Follow From It
cases.rationale: Genuinely hard. Two thirds of the text is expository social analysis with citations; the final third turns into a numbered programme with demands and a call to act. Both functions are strongly present, so the classifier must report LOW CONFIDENCE rather than a confident verdict. The expected destination reflects the dominant final function, but the assertion this case carries is about confidence, not destination.
cases.text:
PART ONE: THE EVIDENCE

It has often been argued that the modern university is in decline. This essay examines the claim rather than assuming it. According to the returns of 1911, the proportion of endowed chairs to enrolled students had fallen by a third within a generation.

For example, at three of the older foundations the teaching staff grew by eleven per cent while admissions more than doubled. The evidence suggests that the strain was structural and not, as the apologists maintain, a temporary effect of the war.

PART TWO: THE ANALYSIS

We shall see that three causes operate together. In the first place the endowments were fixed in nominal terms. In the second, the examination system rewarded volume. Ibid., p. 214. The historian describes the result as drift; the participants experienced it as policy.

It must be shown, and this section attempts to show it, that no single reform addresses all three causes at once.

PART THREE: WHAT MUST FOLLOW

We declare that the present arrangement cannot be defended by anyone who has read the foregoing. We demand the following, and we demand them now.

1. That every chair be funded in real terms and that the endowments be revalued annually.
2. That the examination system be abolished in its present form.
3. That the governing bodies admit those who teach.

Every member of this profession has a duty to press for these measures. Our adversaries are those who profit from the drift and who call it tradition. We reject the counsel of patience that has been offered to us for thirty years.

A new era in the life of these institutions begins on the day this programme is adopted. We call upon every teacher and every student to act, and to act now.
